title: Prevention of cerebral palsy after perinatal brain injury

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment given after brain injury around birth that reliably protects or repairs the developing motor system, allowing newborns at high risk of cerebral palsy to survive without it. Its intended scope includes both term and preterm infants. The central goal is to preserve the development of movement and motor control after an injury has occurred; identifying high-risk infants alone would not satisfy this therapeutic concept. This is a synthesis of the proposed capability, rather than an achievement demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

Two levels of success should remain distinct. Clinical prevention would mean substantially improving survival without cerebral palsy and preserving motor development. Anatomical regeneration would additionally mean reconstructing injured motor pathways, including corticospinal and related connections. Functional improvement, independent walking or typical cognition would not by themselves establish that damaged pathways had been rebuilt. A useful treatment could meet the clinical goal through protection of surviving tissue or functional adaptation without meeting the stricter regeneration goal.

significance.text: The documented treatment gap is substantial. In the supplied cooling trial, treatment after perinatal asphyxia improved childhood outcomes, but mortality and neurological impairment remained common. The cord-blood evidence concerns modest average motor improvements in children who already had cerebral palsy. A treatment that made survival with independent motor development the expected outcome after confirmed perinatal injury would therefore substantially extend the capabilities demonstrated in these sources, especially if benefit were established in a prespecified preterm population.

Conditional impact synthesis: the direct consequence would be fewer deaths and fewer cases of cerebral palsy in the population actually shown to benefit. If effects proved durable, downstream possibilities would include greater independence and reduced need for lifelong assistance and rehabilitation. Their magnitude would depend on treatment eligibility, safety, access and the range of injuries successfully treated. The supplied evidence does not establish what fraction of all cerebral palsy this approach could prevent, and it does not justify claiming that it would eliminate the main biological route into the condition.

The analogy to rebuilding a damaged nervous system has an important limit: a favorable motor outcome is evidence of function, not a reconstruction of the brain's pre-injury architecture. Conversely, an intervention need not reproduce that architecture exactly to deliver a major clinical advance. Preventing cerebral palsy also does not automatically establish typical cognition or the absence of other neurological difficulties; those outcomes require their own assessment.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved target is reliable protection or repair after perinatal injury sufficient to sustain motor development across clearly defined high-risk populations. The supplied cooling study documents benefit in newborns with asphyxial encephalopathy born at 36 weeks or later, with treatment initiated within six hours after birth. Those study conditions define the evidence presented here; they do not establish universal gestational-age or timing limits for every treatment. The study also does not establish efficacy for preterm white-matter injury or demonstrate reconstruction of damaged motor pathways.

Engineering synthesis: a successful intervention would need to reach vulnerable tissue early enough to alter the injury's consequences, preserve or restore the cells and connections needed for motor development, and remain safe in a rapidly developing brain. The stricter regenerative version would additionally need to establish appropriate connections and demonstrate that they support useful motor function. The supplied abstracts do not resolve which mechanisms, delivery methods or treatment windows could accomplish these goals.

A separate demonstration barrier is distinguishing preservation, compensation and reconstruction. Outcome measures must show that treatment changes the child's developmental trajectory rather than merely producing a small short-term score improvement. Selection methods must also identify infants with sufficiently high untreated risk to make prevention interpretable. The proposed MRI-based selection strategy therefore requires prospective validation; the supplied sources do not validate particular MRI patterns or thresholds for this purpose.

current_state.text: Azzopardi and colleagues, published in the New England Journal of Medicine on 10 July 2014, reported outcomes at ages six to seven years after newborns with asphyxial encephalopathy, born at 36 weeks or later, had been randomized to standard care with or without cooling initiated within six hours after birth. Survival with an IQ of at least 85 occurred in 75 of 145 children in the cooling group, or 52%, versus 52 of 132 controls, or 39%. Mortality was 29% versus 30%. Survival without neurological abnormalities was 45% versus 28%. Among survivors, cerebral palsy occurred in 21% versus 36%. These are distinct outcomes with different denominators; the IQ endpoint should not be equated with intact neurological survival.

These cooling results demonstrate partial clinical protection, including a reduction in cerebral palsy among survivors in the studied population. They make an unqualified claim that prevention after perinatal injury has never been achieved misleading. The broader target is reliable prevention in high-risk newborns, with interpretable evidence for preterm infants as well. The retained evidence is a PubMed abstract record, not the full article, and it does not establish anatomical reconstruction, efficacy for preterm white-matter injury or the proportion of cerebral palsy attributable to particular injury types.

Finch-Edmondson and colleagues, published in Pediatrics on 1 May 2025, reported an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of umbilical cord blood treatment in children with established cerebral palsy. The mean advantage on the Gross Motor Function Measure-66 was 1.36 points at six months, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.41–2.32, and 1.42 points at twelve months, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.31–2.52. Younger participants, approximately under five years of age, with milder cerebral palsy showed greater benefit. The retained abstract does not establish that benefit was concentrated specifically in children who could already walk with or without assistance. These findings concern improvement in existing cerebral palsy, not neonatal prevention or demonstrated anatomical regeneration, and should not be generalized to all cell therapies.

The research notes describe iSTOP-CP, linked to NCT07831746, as a phase II intranasal mesenchymal-cell prevention trial that was not yet recruiting and had an estimated 2027 start. However, the supplied review found only generic site text in the retained ClinicalTrials.gov artifact. Its study identity, phase, intervention, recruitment status and projected start therefore remain unverified in this record. This extraction limitation is not evidence that the trial does not exist or that the reported details are false.

Evidence-scope limitation: the supplied review assessed abstract-level records for the two published studies, and the supplied bounded search record is empty. Their dated results can be retained, but this material does not establish a comprehensive account of the field through 1 November 2026. It demonstrates partial benefit from cooling and modest functional improvement from cord blood; it does not demonstrate the full proposed capability, nor does it establish that no other research has achieved broader prevention or anatomical repair.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: enroll newborns using prospectively validated MRI criteria indicating high risk of moderate or severe cerebral palsy, then randomize them to the intervention or an appropriate control. At two years, a standardized examination would show a prespecified, clinically substantial absolute improvement in survival without cerebral palsy, with a large absolute majority of treated infants achieving that outcome. The risk threshold, minimum absolute improvement and numerical meaning of a large majority would be defined before enrollment. These are proposed requirements, not thresholds endorsed by the supplied studies or established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Two-year cerebral-palsy-free survival improves substantially, with a large treated majority

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and reproducibility requirements: include a prespecified preterm stratum with sufficient enrollment and outcome data to yield an interpretable estimate of benefit. Report results by relevant gestational-age and injury groups, treatment timing and baseline risk, together with mortality, adverse effects and losses to follow-up. Independent replication and consistent delivery across clinical sites would strengthen the demonstration. Success in finite study populations would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not universal effectiveness after every perinatal brain injury.
completion_criteria.label: Interpretable preterm benefit estimates with outcomes reported by clinical subgroup

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability requirement: continue follow-up beyond the two-year endpoint to assess later motor function, cognition and other neurological outcomes. A favorable examination at two years would establish an early clinical result, not lifelong normal function. A mean gross-motor score improvement of approximately one to two points in children with established cerebral palsy would not meet the neonatal prevention proposal, although such improvement can still represent a separate therapeutic benefit.
completion_criteria.label: Follow-up beyond two years assesses later neurological outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed stricter regeneration demonstration: add convincing structural and functional evidence that injured motor pathways have been reconstructed, rather than inferring reconstruction from improved performance alone. Appropriate imaging or other ethically obtainable evidence would need to distinguish newly restored pathways from preserved tissue and compensatory routes. The supplied material does not establish a validated method for making that distinction in newborns; anatomical regeneration should therefore remain an additional evidentiary requirement rather than an assumed explanation of clinical success.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Structural and functional evidence demonstrates reconstruction of injured motor pathways

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: PED-04, Controlled reopening of developmental critical periods, overlaps through developmental plasticity and the possibility of changing neurological trajectories. PED-05 concerns intervention after injury around birth to preserve motor development. PED-04 concerns controlled reopening of developmental opportunities later in life. Neither capability automatically establishes the other, and neonatal prevention remains distinct from improving function in established cerebral palsy.

Roster-based synthesis: PED-01, Physiological extrauterine support through fetal organ maturity, shares the context of extreme prematurity and protection of development. Its defining capability is physiological support while organs mature; PED-05 addresses protection or repair after brain injury. Even if extrauterine support eventually reduced injury risk, that would not by itself demonstrate treatment of an injury that had already occurred.

Roster-based synthesis: PED-09, Post-symptomatic restoration of severe genetic neurodevelopmental disorders, shares the ambition of restoring a disrupted developmental trajectory. Its primary target is a genetic disorder after symptoms emerge, whereas PED-05 targets motor development after perinatal injury. PED-06, Prenatal correction that lets severe monogenic disease develop normally, and PED-11, One-time in vivo correction of severe newborn metabolic disease before irreversible injury, likewise emphasize disease-specific correction before substantial damage. Those capabilities could prevent some neurological injury without establishing general repair after perinatal brain injury.

Roster-based synthesis: PED-08, Restoration of nephron endowment after the nephrogenic clock stops, shares the regenerative challenge of recovering developmental capacity after a vulnerable period. The relevant distinction is between restoring an organ's structural complement and rebuilding appropriately connected neural pathways. Evidence that one tissue can regenerate would not establish the corresponding capability in the developing motor system.

change_log.change: Preserved PED-05's identity while separating clinical prevention from anatomical reconstruction.
change_log.reason: Functional recovery can establish a major therapeutic advance without proving that injured motor pathways or pre-injury architecture have been rebuilt.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims about cooling's eligibility limits and inability to rebuild pathways with the documented trial population, timing and evidentiary scope.
change_log.reason: Enrollment at 36 weeks or later and treatment within six hours establish the studied conditions, not universal treatment boundaries or mechanistic impossibility.

change_log.change: Removed deterministic injury-to-cerebral-palsy language and the claim that the innovation would remove cerebral palsy's main biological route.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish inevitable outcomes, the attributable share of particular injuries or population-wide preventability.

change_log.change: Retained the verified 2014 cooling outcomes and clarified the distinct endpoints and survivor denominator for cerebral palsy.
change_log.reason: Survival with IQ of at least 85, survival without neurological abnormalities, mortality and cerebral palsy among survivors are not interchangeable measures.

change_log.change: Corrected the cord-blood subgroup description to younger children with milder cerebral palsy and included the twelve-month confidence interval.
change_log.reason: The reviewed abstract supports age and severity associations, not the earlier specific walking-status claim.

change_log.change: Retained the reported iSTOP-CP details as unverified research-note claims with an explicit extraction limitation.
change_log.reason: The retained ClinicalTrials.gov artifact contains no study details; this prevents verification without establishing that the claims are false.

change_log.change: Reframed the remaining gap as reliable and broader prevention rather than asserting that prevention after injury has never occurred.
change_log.reason: Cooling already reduced cerebral palsy among survivors in the documented trial population.

change_log.change: Made the proposed demonstration operational through prospective risk validation, prespecified thresholds, interpretable preterm results, replication and longer follow-up.
change_log.reason: The original proposal needed defined success criteria and boundaries; two-year outcomes alone do not establish lifelong normal function.

change_log.change: Integrated scientific barriers and relevant roster distinctions as explicitly labeled synthesis.
change_log.reason: The record needs to explain the capability and its boundaries without presenting conceptual reasoning as a finding of the supplied studies.

change_log.change: Qualified the field-wide current-state conclusion and preserved abstract-level access limitations.
change_log.reason: The supplied search record is empty, and the reviewed materials do not establish completeness through 1 November 2026.

unresolved_issues: The identity and reported phase, intervention, recruitment status and projected start of iSTOP-CP at NCT07831746 remain unverified because the retained artifact contains only generic site text.
The supplied material does not establish whether other work had demonstrated broader prevention or anatomical reconstruction by 1 November 2026.
The share of all cerebral palsy potentially preventable through treatment after perinatal brain injury is not established.
The supplied cooling abstract does not settle efficacy for preterm white-matter injury, universal treatment windows or anatomical mechanisms.
Prospectively validated MRI selection criteria, numerical risk thresholds, the minimum absolute benefit and the meaning of a large majority remain to be specified.
A validated, ethically practical way to distinguish reconstructed motor pathways from preserved tissue and compensatory function remains unspecified.
The relationship between two-year prevention outcomes and durable school-age or lifelong neurological function requires longer follow-up.

brief.title: Preventing cerebral palsy after brain injury at birth
possible: After a baby suffers brain injury around birth, treatment could reliably protect or repair the brain systems that control movement. Babies at high risk could survive without cerebral palsy, a condition affecting movement and motor control. The goal includes babies born early and at term.
why: More children could survive with independent movement. Lasting benefits could mean greater independence and less need for lifelong assistance and rehabilitation.

sources.who: Denis Azzopardi and the TOBY Study Group
sources.showed: Cooling newborns after brain injury caused by oxygen deprivation improved childhood outcomes. Cerebral palsy was less common among survivors who received cooling.
sources.quote: Moderate hypothermia after perinatal asphyxia resulted in improved neurocognitive outcomes in middle childhood.
sources.cited_for: Cooling already provides partial protection after brain injury around birth.
sources.not_established: The trial did not establish reliable prevention across high-risk newborns, benefit for preterm brain injury or rebuilt brain connections.

sources.showed: A combined analysis of studies found modest average movement improvements after treatment with blood from the umbilical cord. Younger children with milder cerebral palsy benefited more.
sources.quote: Younger participants (aged approximately <5 years) with milder CP showed increased benefit.
sources.cited_for: Cord blood treatment can improve movement in some children who already have cerebral palsy.
sources.not_established: Improvement in existing cerebral palsy does not establish prevention in newborns or reconstruction of injured brain connections.

sources.showed: A proposed prevention trial would test cell treatment delivered through the nose.
sources.cited_for: The proposed trial concerns treatment intended to prevent cerebral palsy.
sources.not_established: A proposed trial does not establish that the treatment prevents cerebral palsy.

shown: Azzopardi and colleagues demonstrated protection lasting into school age after newborn cooling. Finch-Edmondson and colleagues found modest movement gains from cord blood treatment in children with established cerebral palsy.
missing: Treatment has yet to reliably preserve movement development across clearly defined groups of high-risk newborns, including those born early.
Brain-scan criteria have yet to reliably identify newborns whose untreated risk makes prevention measurable.
Treatment must safely change long-term development, beyond a small improvement on a movement test.
Rebuilding injured movement pathways requires evidence that separates repair from surviving tissue or alternative routes through the brain.

milestones.label: Most treated babies survive without cerebral palsy
milestones.explanation: A randomized trial using validated brain-scan selection would show a substantial benefit at two years, with a large treated majority surviving without cerebral palsy. Preset thresholds would make prevention measurable.

milestones.label: Benefit is measurable in babies born early
milestones.explanation: A trial would include enough preterm babies to estimate benefit and report outcomes, harms and follow-up losses by relevant clinical group. This would establish which groups benefit.

milestones.label: Later follow-up establishes lasting outcomes
milestones.explanation: Follow-up beyond two years would assess movement, thinking and other brain functions. This would reveal whether early prevention translates into lasting benefit.

milestones.label: Injured movement pathways are demonstrably rebuilt
milestones.explanation: Evidence of brain structure and function would distinguish rebuilt movement pathways from preserved tissue and alternative routes. This would establish regeneration beyond improved movement alone.

uncertain: The risk threshold, minimum benefit and meaning of a large treated majority remain to be defined.
An ethically practical way to prove that newborn brain pathways have been rebuilt remains unclear.
The share of all cerebral palsy that treatment after injury could prevent remains unknown.

page.title: Prevention of cerebral palsy after perinatal brain injury
page.definition: Treatment begun after brain injury around birth would help more children survive without cerebral palsy, a permanent disorder of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance in the developing brain. Cooling already provides partial protection for infants born at ≥36 weeks with moderate or severe hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy. The goal extends to infants born earlier and to newborns with arterial ischaemic stroke or preterm white-matter injury.

goal.need: After symptomatic neonatal arterial stroke, 29 of 74 children assessed in a Swiss cohort had cerebral palsy at age two. After asphyxial encephalopathy at ≥36 weeks’ gestation, 21% of cooled survivors and 36% of control survivors assessed at school age had cerebral palsy. Deeper or longer cooling showed no additional benefit against death or disability. Cooling also showed no benefit on that outcome at 33–35 weeks. Effective treatment after these injuries or after preterm white-matter injury could help more children move independently.

figures.caption: Cooling after hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy at 33–35 weeks’ gestation
figures.note: The endpoint was assessed at 18–22 months’ corrected age; 52 examinations occurred later. Outcome denominators differ from randomized totals.

statements.body: Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy Symposium expert panel, reviewed by the Society for Pediatric Research
statements.quote: The next phase of NE clinical trials focuses on adjuvant therapies to hypothermia to further improve neurodevelopmental outcomes.
statements.context: NE means neonatal encephalopathy: disturbed neurological function in the first days after birth. Adjuvant therapies are additional treatments given alongside cooling.

statements.quote: We will evaluate the effectiveness of the therapy based on their motor and cognitive development at the age of 24 months.
statements.context: The proposed iSTOP-CP study compares intranasal donor mesenchymal stromal cells with placebo in 162 newborns with perinatal brain injury.

statements.body: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke and Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
statements.quote: Neurophysiological processes that occur post-injury are potential targets for early intervention and prevention efforts.
statements.context: The Strategic Plan for Cerebral Palsy Research calls for identifying critical periods in brain and motor development when intervention after injury may prevent impairment.

completion.title: Postinjury treatment reduces school-age death or cerebral palsy across the tracked neonatal injury groups.
completion.criterion: In each tracked injury group, treatment begun after documented perinatal brain injury reduces death or cerebral palsy at 6–7 years versus appropriate standard care in randomized evidence: the risk ratio’s 95% confidence interval lies below 1. Cerebral palsy among survivors also decreases on standardized neurological examination. For hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, establish benefit separately in defined cohorts born at ≥36 weeks and <36 weeks. Different treatments may meet the test in different groups.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; no external body was found to define a common completion threshold for this full scope.
completion.basis: COHESION identifies survival and cerebral palsy as core outcomes for neonatal encephalopathy. The school-age confidence limit and the requirement for evidence in each injury group are Atlas choices. In the NICHD trial at ≥36 weeks, death or cerebral palsy at 6–7 years was a secondary outcome: 39/96 with cooling versus 56/93 with usual care, adjusted risk ratio 0.71 (95% CI 0.54–0.95). Among assessed survivors, 12/69 versus 15/52 had cerebral palsy, risk ratio 0.60 (95% CI 0.31–1.18). The iSTOP-CP primary endpoint assesses motor development at two years.

milestones.title: A postinjury treatment improves brain structure and function in at least two animal species.
milestones.criterion: The same treatment, begun after injury, improves both brain histology and neurological function in at least two animal species. Studies reproducibly establish the dose response and treatment window with appropriate physiological monitoring.
milestones.set_by: Stroke Therapy Academic Industry Roundtable, 2009 preclinical recommendations, written for adult stroke; neonatal adaptation discussed in Baby STEPS, 2011.
milestones.threshold_quote: reproducibly defining dose response and time windows with both histological and functional outcomes in multiple animal species with appropriate physiological monitoring is appropriate.

milestones.title: Infants have no treatment-related serious adverse events through three months of age.
milestones.criterion: Observe no treatment-related serious adverse events from neonatal treatment through three months of age. For intranasal mesenchymal stromal cells, PASSIoN also specifies no death within 24 hours of administration, no treatment-related anaphylactic shock and no evidence of treatment-associated cerebral tumour formation on MRI at three months, compared with pretreatment MRI.
milestones.set_by: UMC Utrecht, PASSIoN protocol version 5.1, 16 April 2020, sections 1 and 6.1; written for mesenchymal stromal cells in near-term and term infants with arterial stroke.
milestones.threshold_quote: serious adverse events (SAEs) according to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (chapter 7.2) until the age of 3 months.

milestones.title: A neonatal treatment reduces death or moderate or severe disability at 18–22 months.
milestones.criterion: A randomized trial shows a lower risk of death or protocol-defined moderate or severe disability at 18–22 months, using corrected age for preterm infants. In the 2025 protocol, severe disability means a Bayley-III cognitive score below 70, Gross Motor Function Classification System level III–V, blindness, or inability to hear commands despite amplification. Moderate disability requires a cognitive score of 70–84 plus level II motor function, a treated seizure disorder, or hearing loss requiring amplification or an implant to understand commands.
milestones.set_by: NICHD Neonatal Research Network randomized-trial protocols, 2005 and 2025; written for hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, with different Bayley assessment editions.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary outcome was death or disability (severe or moderate) at 18 to 22 months’ corrected age.

milestones.title: Postinjury treatment improves tissue and functional outcomes in one model of perinatal brain injury.
milestones.criterion: In a rodent or rabbit model relevant to the neonatal injury, treatment begun after injury improves both a histological measure of brain injury and a behavioural measure of function compared with injured controls.
milestones.set_by: Stroke Therapy Academic Industry Roundtable initial-testing recommendations for stroke, applied to perinatal injury models with the neonatal translational guidance in Baby STEPS.
milestones.threshold_quote: using both histological and behavioral outcome measurements. Rodents or rabbits are acceptable for initial testing

milestones.title: Fewer treated survivors in a randomized cohort have cerebral palsy at 6–7 years.
milestones.criterion: At 6–7 years, assess cerebral palsy by structured neurological examination and compare its prevalence among assessed survivors by original randomized group. Prevalence is lower in the treatment group at a two-sided P value below 0.05. Report mortality by group so the survivor comparison can be interpreted.
milestones.set_by: TOBY Children Study follow-up protocol and statistical analysis for infants born at ≥36 weeks with asphyxial encephalopathy. Cerebral-palsy prevalence was a prespecified secondary outcome, with no adjustment for multiple secondary comparisons.
milestones.threshold_quote: A two-sided P value of less than 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

not_found: No common externally specified completion threshold or minimum absolute benefit was found for postinjury prevention across the three injury groups.
No randomized postinjury treatment result with school-age cerebral-palsy outcomes was verified for perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke or preterm white-matter injury.
No NIH research priority or professional-society statement reviewed disputes the goal of preventing cerebral palsy after perinatal brain injury.

results.finding: PASSIoN: 10 neonates with perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke received intranasal MSCs; 0 had serious adverse events through 3 months.
results.detail: Follow-up MRI showed no unexpected structural abnormalities, including tumour formation. One infant had a mild transient fever. The study was uncontrolled and could not exclude rare or late adverse events.
results.quote: No serious adverse events were observed.

results.finding: Among 10 infants treated after stroke, 3 (30%) had an abnormal early motor assessment.
results.detail: The study was single-arm and assessed motor function at 4 months. It did not test death or protocol-defined disability at 18–22 months in a randomized comparison.
results.quote: Abnormal early motor assessment was found in three (30%) infants.

results.finding: TOBY randomized 325 newborns with asphyxial encephalopathy. At 6–7 years, cerebral palsy affected 21% of assessed cooled survivors versus 36% of controls.
results.detail: The supplied text does not give the survivor denominators for the cerebral palsy comparison.
results.quote: Among survivors, children in the hypothermia group, as compared with those in the control group, had significant reductions in the risk of cerebral palsy (21% vs. 36%, P=0.03) and the risk of moderate or severe disability (22% vs. 37%, P=0.03); they also had significantly better motor-function scores.

results.finding: In 17 near-term fetal sheep, delayed head cooling reduced parasagittal cortical neuronal loss by 48 percentage points versus sham cooling.
results.detail: The functional outcome was EEG recovery. Behavioral function was unmeasured.
results.quote: Hypothermia was associated with better recovery of electroencephalographic activity (-8.9% +/- 1.8 decibels) and substantially reduced neuronal loss in the parasagittal cortex (46 +/- 13%), the lateral cortex (9 +/- 4%), and other regions except the cornu ammonis sectors 1 and 2 of the hippocampus.

results.finding: In 20 injured neonatal rats, delayed cooling reduced MRI-measured infarct size by 23% and improved spatial memory.
results.detail: The reported improvements in circling and treadmill performance did not reach statistical significance.
results.quote: Hypothermia significantly reduced the final size of cerebral infarction by 23% at 6 wk after the insult.

results.finding: In 20 injured neonatal rats, one delayed cooling regimen reduced MRI-measured infarct size by 23% and improved spatial memory.
results.quote: Hypothermia significantly reduced the final size of cerebral infarction by 23% at 6 wk after the insult.

results.finding: In 236 neonatal rats assessed after moderate hypoxia–ischaemia, immediate cooling provided about 40% protection against hemispheric area loss at one week.
results.detail: The study measured weight gain but did not directly assess feeding behaviour or sensorimotor function.
results.quote: Median hemispheric area loss of the left side was 54.6% in the NT group, with around 40% neuroprotection in the HT33.5, HT32, and HT30 groups

results.finding: In 236 neonatal rats assessed after moderate hypoxia–ischaemia, cooling depth produced a U-shaped tissue response with about 40% hemispheric neuroprotection at protective temperatures.
results.detail: Sentinel pups tracked rectal temperature. The experiments repeatedly included the 37 °C control and 32 °C cooling groups, with treatment always starting immediately after hypoxia.
results.quote: Across the hypothermia treatment groups, a temperature-dependent U-shaped curve of neuroprotection was seen

results.finding: In neonatal stroke rats given erythropoietin-pre-exposed stromal cells (n=10), the histological hemisphere volume ratio improved versus vehicle (P<0.0001).
results.detail: The day-3 cell group also showed more symmetric forelimb lifts versus injured controls (P<0.001).
results.quote: In this study EPO enhanced long-term brain volume and recognition memory when initiated at either day 3 or day 7, similar to MSC/EPO, but only EPO3 animals had improved locomotion, exploratory behavior and reduced anxiety in OF testing with day 7 treatment.

results.finding: In neonatal stroke rats starting systemic erythropoietin on day 7 (n=11), recognition memory improved versus injured vehicle controls (P<0.01).
results.detail: The tested systemic regimen was 1,000 units/kg per dose, given three times at 72-hour intervals.
results.quote: In this study EPO enhanced long-term brain volume and recognition memory when initiated at either day 3 or day 7, similar to MSC/EPO, but only EPO3 animals had improved locomotion, exploratory behavior and reduced anxiety in OF testing with day 7 treatment.

results.finding: High-dose cells reduced forepaw-use asymmetry after neonatal stroke in mice (14 treated vs 18 vehicle, P < 0.05) and reduced peri-infarct microgliosis.
results.detail: Hemispheric volume loss persisted. The rotarod and open-field tests showed no significant group differences.
results.quote: After administration of high-dose UC-MSCs, performance in the cylinder test was significantly improved in comparison to the performance of the vehicle mice.

results.finding: In neonatal stroke mice (5 per group for histology), high-dose cells reduced peri-infarct Iba1 staining. The low-dose comparison showed a trend (P = 0.083).
results.detail: Hemispheric volume did not improve. Systemic blood flow was monitored for 10 minutes after infusion and cerebral blood flow was assessed 24 hours later.
results.quote:
In the peri-infarct cortex, high-dose UC-MSCs significantly reduced the Iba1-positive percent area, and low-dose UC-MSCs also showed the same trend toward reduction (
p
= 0.083).

results.finding: In neonatal mice with diffuse white-matter injury, intranasal stem cells reduced forepaw preference versus vehicle (12 treated, 14 controls, P = 0.003).
results.detail: The same dose of 500,000 cells improved both outcomes. Hippocampal area loss persisted.
results.quote: Intranasal MSC treatment boosts myelination and rescues motor and cognitive impairments in dWMI mice.

results.finding: In neonatal mice with diffuse white-matter injury, day-3 intranasal stem cells restored myelin fibre length (14 treated, 13 vehicle controls, P = 0.039).
results.detail: Rat-derived cell cultures supplied mechanistic evidence. The whole-animal treatment experiments were in mice.
results.quote: Fiber length, a microstructural myelin parameter, was restored in dWMI animals that received MSC treatment at 3 days after injury induction.

results.finding: Postinjury mesenchymal stem cells increased subcortical myelination in preterm fetal sheep versus injured saline controls (n=6 per group, P=0.007).
results.quote: Intravenous MSC administration significantly increased (HI-SAL vs. HI-MSC; P=0.007) myelination

results.finding: Postinjury mesenchymal stem cells reduced electrographic seizure counts in preterm fetal sheep versus injured saline controls (n=6 per group, p=0.031).
results.quote: Intravenous MSC administration significantly reduced (HI-SAL vs. HI-MSC p=0.031) the number of electrographic seizures during the study period after global HI

results.finding: Six cooled neonates with hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy had 0 serious adverse events after intravenous stromal cell treatment.
results.detail: Two nonserious events were reported. A positive culture from a thawed product sample was attributed to contamination during handling, and the infant showed no infection. A separate infant had a transient bloody stool attributed to likely milk protein allergy.
results.quote: Infusions were well tolerated and no acute toxicity or serious adverse events were noted in the 12 months of follow-up.

results.finding: Among six neonates with hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy treated with intravenous stromal cells and cooling, 0 died during follow-up.
results.quote: All babies survived, with average to low-average developmental assessment standard scores for ages between 12 and 17 postnatal months.

results.finding: Among 10 infants treated with intranasal stromal cells after perinatal arterial stroke, 0 treatment-related adverse events were reported by age 2 years.
results.detail: The post hoc adverse-event analysis covered the period after 3 months. The MRI analysis measured tissue loss, and the paper refers readers to the original trial report for the acute safety outcomes.
results.quote: By the age of 2 years, no related adverse events were reported.

results.finding: At age 2 years, motor scores favored children treated with intranasal stromal cells after stroke (n=10) over registry comparators (n=39), P=0.003.
results.quote:
The motor performance score of the PASSIoN cohort was significantly higher than the registry cohort (median
Z
score 0.3 (0.8) versus −0.4 (1.5);
P
=0.003), with 0% and 33% of children having a motor delay, respectively.

results.finding: At age 2 years, cerebral palsy was less frequent after intranasal stromal cells (n=10) than in the registry cohort (n=39), P=0.16.
results.quote:
At neurodevelopmental follow-up at the age of 2 years, the rate of CP was 20% versus 49% (
P
=0.16) between the PASSIoN and registry cohort (Table
3
).

results.finding: In 208 randomized infants with hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, adverse events were similar between groups during 72 hours of cooling.
results.detail: The report gives no event counts, severity breakdown, or attribution to treatment for this comparison.
results.quote: Adverse events were similar in the two groups during the 72 hours of cooling.

results.finding: In 205 infants with hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy and outcome data, whole-body cooling reduced death or moderate or severe disability at 18–22 months (risk ratio 0.72).
results.quote: Death or moderate or severe disability occurred in 45 of 102 infants (44 percent) in the hypothermia group and 64 of 103 infants (62 percent) in the control group (risk ratio, 0.72; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.54 to 0.95; P=0.01).

results.finding: In 168 randomized preterm infants with hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, the adjusted risk ratio for death or moderate or severe disability with cooling was 1.11.
results.detail: Cooling targeted 33.5 °C for 72 hours. Delayed assessments occurred at 23–40 months’ corrected age.
results.quote: aRR using neutral prior probability was 1.11 (95% CrI, 0.74-2.00), yielding probability of benefit, 26%, and of harm, 74%

results.finding: Among preterm infants with hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy assigned to cooling, major bleeding occurred in 1 of 88 during the intervention.
results.detail: The main nondeath safety comparison covered the intervention period, with selected additional outcomes reported for the hospitalization.

results.finding: Neonatal rats (n unreported) had histological and behavioural benefits with shorter cooling versus 5 hours.
results.quote: Across analyses, both 2- and 3-hour hypothermia durations provided greater neuroprotection than 5 hours-including brain lesion volume, motor and cognitive performances, and markers of neuronal preservation and neuroinflammation.

results.finding: Neonatal rats (n unreported) showed the strongest overall neuroprotection with 2 hours of postinjury cooling.
results.quote: However, for several parameters, 2 hours of hypothermia showed superior efficacy compared with 3 hours. Immediate initiation further modestly improved outcomes.

results.finding: Treated neonatal rats with preterm white-matter injury outperformed injured controls on rotarod and passive avoidance tests (n = 8 per group, all P < 0.05).
results.detail: The study used 120 pups overall and reported a 15% exclusion rate. Sample sizes varied by outcome.
results.quote: It also alleviated OPC maturation arrest and preserved the complexity of myelinated axons in the white matter, leading to cognitive, motor and behavioral functional improvements.

results.finding: Neonatal rats given mesenchymal stem cells after injury improved on rotarod and passive avoidance tests (n = 8 per group, all P < 0.05).
results.detail: The experiment evaluated one intracerebroventricular dose of 5 × 10⁴ cells at 24 hours after injury.
results.quote: MSC treatment mitigated neuronal death, protected against injury in both the cortex and white matter, improved neurological and behavioral outcomes, and elevated neuroserpin and N-cadherin levels in neurons.

results.finding: In rats with germinal matrix haemorrhage, delayed intranasal stromal cells restored striatal myelin-positive area (n = 60 across three groups, q = 0.0003).
results.detail: The sample size is inferred from the reported one-way ANOVA degrees of freedom (2, 57).
results.quote:
Specifically, the GMH 
induced reduction in MBP-positive white matter area 
of the striatum (q = 0.0001) was recovered by HuMSC 
treatment (q = 0.0003; Fig.  7a).

results.finding: Delayed intranasal stromal cells improved myelin measures in two rat models, including striatal staining after haemorrhage (n = 60 across three groups, q = 0.0003).
results.detail: The sample size is inferred from the haemorrhage-model ANOVA degrees of freedom. In the inflammation model, the transcriptomic score showed no monotonic dose response.
results.quote:
Across treat -
ments and models, we found that HuMSCs at 50 M cells/
kg BW, when administered in the tertiary phase (15 days) 
after injury via the IN route, were the most effective at 
reducing white and grey matter injury (Table  4, bold).

results.finding: Among 14 neonates with HIE randomized to Temcell plus cooling or cooling alone, 0 severe adverse events were reported.
results.detail: The first intravenous Temcell dose was given 12–36 hours after birth. The paper does not specify a three-month safety cutoff or tabulate serious adverse events separately.
results.quote: but none were severe, and there were no deaths.

results.finding: Among 13 assessed infants with HIE, the 18-month Kyoto response rate was 9.5 percentage points higher with Temcell plus cooling.
results.detail: One Temcell recipient was excluded from efficacy analysis after a protocol deviation. The blinded committee's overall response assessment was 4/6 with Temcell plus cooling and 5/7 with cooling alone.
results.quote:
66.7% (4/6) of the patients in the Temcell combination 
group and 57.1% (4/7) of those in the hypothermia therapy-alone group were responsive to treatment

results.finding: Among 9 preterm infants treated with intraventricular stromal cells after periventricular hemorrhagic infarction, 0 serious adverse events were reported.
results.detail: The cohort had focal hemorrhagic periventricular injury. Follow-up included term-equivalent age and annual assessments through corrected age 5 years, with no dedicated three-month visit described.
results.quote: We observed no serious short- or long-term adverse events, including tumorigenicity or ectopic tissue formation.

results.finding: Among 9 treated preterm infants with periventricular hemorrhagic infarction, 6 had a Bayley-II Mental Developmental Index below 70 at corrected age 2 years.
results.detail: The comparison by baseline injury severity was post hoc. The developmental assessment used Bayley-II rather than the Bayley-III cognitive scale specified in the 2025 protocol.
results.quote: At CA 2 years, all infants in the PVHI score 3 group showed a BSID-II MDI score <70 compared with one infant (25%) in the PVHI score 2 group ( P  = .048).

results.finding: Among 9 treated preterm survivors of periventricular hemorrhagic infarction, 8 had cerebral palsy at corrected age 5 years.
Intranasal mesenchymal stem cells improved cylinder rearing in neonatal mice with diffuse white-matter injury (12 treated, 14 vehicle, P = 0.003).
results.detail: Treated mice also improved on the T-maze at postnatal day 26 (8 treated, 4 vehicle, P = 0.029). Hippocampal area loss persisted after treatment.
results.quote: Intranasal MSC treatment boosts myelination and rescues motor and cognitive impairments in dWMI mice.

results.finding: Intranasal mesenchymal stem cells restored myelin fibre length in mice with diffuse white-matter injury (14 treated, 13 vehicle, P = 0.039).
results.quote: Fiber length, a microstructural myelin parameter, was restored in dWMI animals that received MSC treatment at 3 days after injury induction.

results.finding: Among 10 neonates treated with intranasal mesenchymal stromal cells after perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke, 0 had serious adverse events through three months of age.
results.detail: The sample of ten infants limits detection of rare adverse events.
results.quote:
Regarding safety, no serious 
adverse events were observed in our ten patients, who 
were followed up for safety outcomes until the age 
of 3 months.

results.finding: In preterm infants with hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, major bleeding occurred in 1 of 88 assigned to cooling.
results.detail: Major bleeding prompted blood product administration. The report does not attribute the event to cooling or provide a complete safety assessment through three months.

results.finding: In 168 randomized preterm infants with hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, the adjusted risk ratio for death or moderate or severe disability with cooling was 1.11.
results.detail: Primary outcome data were available for 152 infants. Pandemic restrictions delayed follow-up for 52 infants, whose assessments occurred at 23–40 months’ corrected age.
results.quote: aRR using neutral prior probability was 1.11 (95% CrI, 0.74-2.00), yielding probability of benefit, 26%, and of harm, 74%

results.finding: Female neonatal rats had better sensorimotor scores after postinjury cooling (p < 0.0007). The six-week cohort had 61 survivors, with female subgroup size unreported.
results.detail: The abstract gives the six-week cohort size but omits the number of females in each treatment arm.

but in female pups the total functional score was higher in the hypothermia group(150 ± 35
versus
100 ± 34,
p
< 0.0007) which corresponded to a marked (51%) reduction of the neuropathology score in this subgroup.

results.finding: In endotoxin-exposed rabbit kits (69 assigned), postinjury D-NAC improved myelin staining and locomotion versus injured PBS controls (locomotion P ≤ 0.01).
results.detail: Locomotion scores were based on steps and hops without falls. Histology quantified myelinated area per hemisphere using myelin basic protein staining.
results.quote:
Intravenous administration of a single 10 mg/kg dose of D-NAC resulted in a significant
improvement in neuronal injury and motor function in CP kits (movie S3)

results.finding: After prenatal hypoxia–ischemia, erythropoietin-treated rats (n = 12) recovered gait, with a mean stride length of 8.71 cm.
results.detail: The in vivo study tested one dose and one dosing schedule. Gait group sizes follow the Methods and Results text, which agree. The Figure 6 caption reverses the vehicle and sham counts.
results.quote:
Importantly, TSHI-EPO rats had stride length (8.71 ± 0.44 cm,
n
= 12) and step frequency (3.59 ± 0.24 steps/s) indistinguishable from shams.

results.finding: In 22 randomized preterm infants with periventricular hemorrhagic infarction, stromal cells yielded an RR of 0.45 for Bayley-III cognitive scores below 70 among 17 survivors.
results.detail: The cognitive result was exploratory and its confidence interval included no effect. The primary endpoint was shunt placement or death by 36 weeks’ postmenstrual age.

definition = "Treatment begun after brain injury around birth would help more children survive without cerebral palsy, a permanent disorder of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance in the developing brain. Cooling already provides partial protection for infants born at \u226536 weeks with moderate or severe hypoxic\u2013ischaemic encephalopathy. The goal extends to infants born earlier and to newborns with arterial ischaemic stroke or preterm white-matter injury.". Reason: The current definition presents benefit across term and preterm populations as established and leaves the population with demonstrated protection unspecified.

goal.need = "After symptomatic neonatal arterial stroke, 29 of 74 children assessed in a Swiss cohort had cerebral palsy at age two. After asphyxial encephalopathy at \u226536 weeks\u2019 gestation, 21% of cooled survivors and 36% of control survivors assessed at school age had cerebral palsy. Deeper or longer cooling showed no additional benefit against death or disability. Cooling also showed no benefit on that outcome at 33\u201335 weeks. Effective treatment after these injuries or after preterm white-matter injury could help more children move independently.". Reason: The current rationale gives a motor-score result in children who already have cerebral palsy but omits the risk after neonatal stroke and the tested limits of cooling.

add statement by National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke and Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, 2017: "Neurophysiological processes that occur post-injury are potential targets for early intervention and prevention efforts.". Reason: The 2017 joint NIH strategic plan explicitly identifies prevention after injury as a research priority.

edit completion: basis = "COHESION identifies survival and cerebral palsy as core outcomes for neonatal encephalopathy. The school-age confidence limit and the requirement for evidence in each injury group are Atlas choices. In the NICHD trial at \u226536 weeks, death or cerebral palsy at 6\u20137 years was a secondary outcome: 39/96 with cooling versus 56/93 with usual care, adjusted risk ratio 0.71 (95% CI 0.54\u20130.95). Among assessed survivors, 12/69 versus 15/52 had cerebral palsy, risk ratio 0.60 (95% CI 0.31\u20131.18). The iSTOP-CP primary endpoint assesses motor development at two years."; refs = [1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 30, 31]. Reason: The basis omits the consensus on which outcomes to report and the randomized result that already meets the composite threshold in one gestational cohort.

add milestone after None: "Postinjury treatment improves tissue and functional outcomes in one model of perinatal brain injury.". Reason: The sequence starts with replication across species and skips the initial demonstration of tissue and functional benefit in one animal model.

edit m1: criterion = "The same treatment, begun after injury, improves both brain histology and neurological function in at least two animal species. Studies reproducibly establish the dose response and treatment window with appropriate physiological monitoring.". Reason: The mouse experiment embedded in the criterion cannot by itself establish replication across species.

edit m2: title = "Infants have no treatment-related serious adverse events through three months of age."; criterion = "Observe no treatment-related serious adverse events from neonatal treatment through three months of age. For intranasal mesenchymal stromal cells, PASSIoN also specifies no death within 24 hours of administration, no treatment-related anaphylactic shock and no evidence of treatment-associated cerebral tumour formation on MRI at three months, compared with pretreatment MRI."; threshold_quote = "serious adverse events (SAEs) according to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (chapter 7.2) until the age of 3 months."; threshold_ref = 11. Reason: PASSIoN specifies three months of age as the safety endpoint, and its enrolment and two-year outcomes are results rather than parts of that test.

edit m3: criterion = "A randomized trial shows a lower risk of death or protocol-defined moderate or severe disability at 18\u201322 months, using corrected age for preterm infants. In the 2025 protocol, severe disability means a Bayley-III cognitive score below 70, Gross Motor Function Classification System level III\u2013V, blindness, or inability to hear commands despite amplification. Moderate disability requires a cognitive score of 70\u201384 plus level II motor function, a treated seizure disorder, or hearing loss requiring amplification or an implant to understand commands."; threshold_quote = "The primary outcome was death or disability (severe or moderate) at 18 to 22 months\u2019 corrected age."; threshold_ref = 2. Reason: The criterion mixes two trials’ results with the endpoint and omits the corrected-age qualification of the preterm protocol.

add milestone after m3: "Fewer treated survivors in a randomized cohort have cerebral palsy at 6–7 years.". Reason: A lower infant disability composite can occur without fewer cases of cerebral palsy, and TOBY prespecified a direct school-age comparison among survivors.
remove not found 3. Reason: The joint NINDS/NICHD strategic plan is available in full and its postinjury prevention recommendation can be quoted directly.

remove not found 2. Reason: The sponsor record reproduced by Veeva identifies the primary motor endpoint and shows why the phase needs qualification: the structured fields list phases 2 and 3, while the study description calls it phase II.

add not found: "No NIH research priority or professional-society statement reviewed disputes the goal of preventing cerebral palsy after perinatal brain injury.". Reason: The distinction between objections to a specific therapy and disagreement with the prevention goal matters when interpreting the negative preterm cooling trial.
